title: Grade 4 AGRICULTURE — 3.3 Cleaning Personal Protective Equipment

pages.lesson:
PAGE 1: Overview

OVERVIEW
========

Personal protective equipment only protects you when it is clean and in good condition. In this sub-strand you will identify gloves, dust masks, gumboots, headgear, overalls and canvas shoes, learn how to clean them, and display clean equipment as a reminder that hygiene includes the things you wear for work.

## Strand 3.0: Hygiene Practices
Sub-strand 3.3: Cleaning Personal Protective Equipment
Suggested lessons: 9

## Learning outcomes
By the end of the sub-strand, the learner should be able to:
a) identify personal protective equipment in day to day life
b) clean personal protective equipment for hygiene purposes
c) appreciate clean personal protective equipment in promoting hygiene

## Key inquiry questions
1. How does cleaning of personal protective equipment promote hygiene?

## Core competencies
• Digital literacy: use of digital technology as learners search for information on personal protective equipment.

## Values
• Responsibility: safety and care of self as learners clean personal protective equipment.

## Pertinent and contemporary issues
• Personal safety as learners exercise caution while undertaking cleaning activity.

## Links to other learning areas
• Learners relate use of personal protective equipment to personal safety skills learnt in Science and Technology.

## Source
• KICD Grade 4 Agriculture Curriculum Design (Revised 2024) — Strand 3.0 Hygiene Practices, Sub-strand 3.3 Cleaning Personal Protective Equipment

PAGE 2: Lesson 1: What personal protective equipment is

LESSON 1: WHAT PERSONAL PROTECTIVE EQUIPMENT IS
===============================================

## What you will learn
• Explain what personal protective equipment is.
• Name the common items used in day-to-day work.

Curriculum outcomes: a) identify personal protective equipment in day to day life

## Introduction
Before you handle compost, sweep a dusty store or walk through a muddy pen, you put something on so that the dirt meets the equipment first. That clothing and gear is personal protective equipment.

## Notes
Personal protective equipment, shortened to PPE, is what you wear to protect your body while you work. It is personal because it guards the wearer. It is protective because it stops injuries and blocks mud, dust, thorns and waste. In day-to-day life at home, at school and on the farm, the items you should be able to name are gloves, dust masks, gumboots, headgear, overalls and canvas shoes.

Each item covers a different part of the body. Gloves cover the hands. A dust mask covers the nose and mouth. Gumboots and canvas shoes cover the feet. Headgear covers the hair and shades the head. An overall covers the clothes and much of the body. You do not need every item for every job. You need the item that matches the risk.

PPE is also a hygiene matter. Dirt that stays on your shirt or under your nails travels into the house and onto food. Equipment that catches that dirt can be removed and cleaned at the door. In that way, protective equipment supports the personal hygiene and domestic hygiene you have already studied.

The equipment must be the right size. Gloves that fall off do not protect. Gumboots that are far too big can make you trip. A mask that does not cover the nose is only a decoration. Equipment must also be whole. A hole in a glove lets dirt straight onto the skin.

You may see other protective items on adults, such as goggles or helmets, in workshops and on building sites. In this sub-strand, concentrate on the six everyday items so that you can identify them in real work and know which ones you will learn to clean.

Look around the school store, the garden and your home. Point to each item by its proper name before you use it.

## Key words
• personal protective equipment — gear worn to protect the body during work
• PPE — the short name for personal protective equipment

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Name the PPE that protects the hands, the feet in mud, and the nose during dusty work.

Working:
1. Hands are covered by gloves.
2. Feet in mud are protected by gumboots.
3. The nose and mouth are protected by a dust mask.

Answer: Gloves, gumboots and a dust mask.

## Activity: Identify protective equipment
You will need: Real items or pictures of gloves, dust masks, gumboots, headgear, an overall and canvas shoes, Exercise book
1. Observe each item and name it.
2. Say which part of the body it protects.
3. Search a school poster, a book or a digital device, if one is available, for one more fact about that item.
4. Write the six names and one job for each.

## Practice
1. What is personal protective equipment?
2. List six common PPE items in day-to-day work.
3. Why does PPE need to fit and to be free of holes?

## Summary
• PPE protects the body during work.
• The everyday items are gloves, dust masks, gumboots, headgear, overalls and canvas shoes.
• Each item must fit and be in good condition.

### Answers to practice
1. Gear worn to protect the body while working.
2. Gloves, dust masks, gumboots, headgear, overalls and canvas shoes.
3. If it falls off or has holes, dirt and injury can still reach the body.

PAGE 3: Lesson 2: Gloves, dust masks and headgear

LESSON 2: GLOVES, DUST MASKS AND HEADGEAR
=========================================

## What you will learn
• Describe gloves, dust masks and headgear.
• Match each item to suitable work.

Curriculum outcomes: a) identify personal protective equipment in day to day life

## Introduction
Hands, lungs and hair meet dirt in different ways. A glove does not stop dust you breathe, and a hat does not keep compost off your fingers. You choose the item for the part of the body at risk.

## Notes
Gloves protect the hands from dirt, thorns, rough stalks and waste. Garden gloves are often made of cloth or rubber. Rubber gloves are better when the work is wet. Cloth gloves are better for dry weeding, but they soak up water and then hold dirt against the skin. Gloves do not replace hand washing. When you pull them off, your hands can still pick up what was on the outside, so you wash with soap afterwards.

A dust mask covers the nose and mouth. It reduces the dust you breathe when you sweep a dry store, shake dry fodder or work where fine dust rises. It is not a swimming mask and it is not medicine. A cloth mask can be washed. Some thin dust masks are meant to be thrown away when they are dusty, wet or torn. A mask that has gaps at the sides lets dust pass. Do not share masks. Do not wear a mask that is so dirty you are breathing through mud.

Headgear means a cap, hat or clean headscarf worn for work. It keeps dust, seeds and dry leaves out of the hair and shades the head from strong sun. Hair that is covered is also less likely to drop into food if you move from the garden to helping in the kitchen, though you still wash your hands. Headgear for work should be washable. A school hat and a work hat can be the same kind of item, but a hat used in a dirty pen should be cleaned before it is worn to a meal.

These three items are often forgotten because the work looks small. Pulling weeds still drives soil under the nails. Sweeping a store still fills the air with dust. Name the item, wear it for the right job, and take it off before you sit down to eat.

## Key words
• gloves — coverings worn on the hands during dirty or rough work
• headgear — a cap, hat or headscarf worn to protect the head and hair

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Which items fit these jobs: sorting dry maize in a dusty store, washing a muddy tool, weeding under a hot sun?

Working:
1. Dusty sorting needs a dust mask.
2. A muddy wash needs gloves, preferably ones that can get wet.
3. Hot sun and hair full of bits of plant call for headgear.

Answer: Dust mask for the store, gloves for the muddy tool, headgear for weeding in the sun.

## Activity: Match three items to real jobs
You will need: Gloves, Dust mask, Cap or headscarf, Job cards
1. Lay the three items on the table and observe how each is worn.
2. Match them to jobs the class suggests from home and school.
3. Practise putting gloves on and taking them off without touching the dirty side with your bare palm as much as you can.
4. Wash your hands after the demonstration.

## Practice
1. Why do you wash your hands after taking off gloves?
2. When should a disposable dust mask be thrown away?
3. What does headgear protect you from during garden work?

## Summary
• Gloves protect hands, masks reduce dust breathed in, and headgear covers the hair.
• Choose the item that matches the job.
• Do not share masks, and wash hands after removing gloves.

### Answers to practice
1. Dirt from the outside of the gloves can get onto your skin as you remove them.
2. When it is dusty, wet or torn.
3. Sun, dust and bits of plants in the hair.

PAGE 4: Lesson 3: Gumboots, overalls and canvas shoes

LESSON 3: GUMBOOTS, OVERALLS AND CANVAS SHOES
=============================================

## What you will learn
• Describe gumboots, overalls and canvas shoes.
• Choose footwear and body covering for wet and dry work.

Curriculum outcomes: a) identify personal protective equipment in day to day life

## Introduction
Canvas shoes are light and useful on a dry path. They are a poor choice in a flooded pen. Gumboots are the opposite. Knowing the difference keeps your feet and your clothes clean.

## Notes
Gumboots are waterproof boots, usually rubber, that cover the foot and the lower leg. Wear them in mud, wet grass, animal houses, and places where sharp rubbish or hidden stones may cut an open shoe. Tuck long trousers into them or wear them under an overall so that mud does not run down inside. Gumboots that are full of yesterday's mud are not protecting hygiene. They are carrying the pen into the house.

An overall is a garment worn over ordinary clothes. It takes splashes, dust and dung so that your uniform or home clothes stay clean. Button or zip it properly. Sleeves that flap can catch on tools. After dirty work, take the overall off before you sit on a bed or a classroom chair. If you only own an apron, use the apron in the same spirit: it is body covering for the front of your clothes during cleaning or cooking.

Canvas shoes are cloth shoes with a rubber sole. They suit dry sweeping, classroom duties and dry garden work. They are cooler and lighter than gumboots. They are not waterproof. Wet canvas holds water, dries slowly and can smell if it is left in a bag. Wear socks so that the shoe does not rub the skin. Canvas shoes used as PPE should be kept for work if you can, so that the pair you wear to a clean room stays cleaner.

Choose footwear by looking at the ground. Dry and fairly clean ground: canvas shoes. Mud, dung or water: gumboots. Add the overall when the whole body, not only the feet, will meet dirt. School uniform alone is not protective equipment for a cowshed.

All three items last longer when they are cleaned and dried after use. The next lessons show how. For identification, you should be able to point to each one and say what work it is for.

## Key words
• gumboots — waterproof rubber boots that protect the feet and lower legs
• canvas shoes — light cloth shoes with rubber soles for dry work
• overall — a garment worn over clothes to keep them clean

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A learner wears canvas shoes and a school uniform to wash out a muddy goat pen. What is wrong with the choice?

Working:
1. The ground is wet and dirty.
2. Canvas shoes soak up muddy water.
3. The uniform has no covering, so it will carry dirt back to the house.

Answer: Gumboots and an overall would protect the feet and clothes. Canvas shoes and uniform are for cleaner, drier work.

## Activity: Choose footwear and covering for two jobs
You will need: Pictures or real gumboots, canvas shoes and an overall, Two job cards: dry sweeping and washing a pen
1. Observe how gumboots, canvas shoes and an overall are made.
2. Decide which to wear for dry sweeping and which for a wet pen.
3. Explain your choice to another pair of learners.
4. List one problem caused by wearing the wrong shoes.

## Practice
1. When are gumboots a better choice than canvas shoes?
2. What is the job of an overall?
3. Why are wet canvas shoes a hygiene problem if they are left in a closed bag?

## Summary
• Gumboots are for wet and muddy work. Canvas shoes are for dry work.
• An overall keeps dirt off your clothes.
• Choose the covering that matches the ground and the job.

### Answers to practice
1. In mud, water, animal houses and places with sharp rubbish.
2. To cover ordinary clothes so that dirt from work does not spoil them.
3. They stay damp and start to smell, and they do not dry.

PAGE 5: Lesson 4: Why protective equipment must be cleaned

LESSON 4: WHY PROTECTIVE EQUIPMENT MUST BE CLEANED
==================================================

## What you will learn
• Explain how dirty PPE spreads dirt and germs.
• Give reasons for cleaning equipment after work.

Curriculum outcomes: a) identify personal protective equipment in day to day life; c) appreciate clean personal protective equipment in promoting hygiene

## Introduction
Gumboots caked with dung do not stop being dirty when you step into the kitchen. If the dirt is not washed off, the equipment carries the pen, the store or the latrine into the next place.

## Notes
Cleaning PPE promotes hygiene because it removes the dirt the equipment was worn to catch. That dirt may include soil, animal droppings, food waste, grease and dust. Germs travel with it. A dirty glove on a clean table, or a dusty mask on a bed, undoes the washing you did on your hands and the sweeping you did on the floor.

There are four clear reasons to clean the equipment. First, clean PPE does not spread germs to people, food and furniture. Second, it protects you better next time. A blocked mask is hard to breathe through, and a greasy glove slips. Third, clean equipment lasts longer. Mud left on rubber cracks and rots cloth. Fourth, you can see damage once the dirt is off. A nail in a boot, a hole in a glove or a torn strap shows up on a clean item.

Cleaning also shows respect for the next user. At school, gumboots and gloves may be shared across groups. The group that finishes must leave them fit for the group that follows. That is part of caring for other learners' safety.

Dirty equipment should be cleaned outside or in a washing area, not on the kitchen table and not in the drinking-water basin. Scrape dry mud off first so that you do not waste water. Use soap where the item allows it. Dry the item before you store it. Folding a wet overall into a plastic bag keeps it sour.

Appreciate clean PPE by treating it as part of the job, not as an extra you skip when you are tired. The last minutes of work are washing the boots, hanging the overall and washing your own hands. Then the house stays as clean as you left it.

## Key words
• contaminate — to spread dirt or germs onto something clean
• store — to keep equipment in a set place when it is not being worn

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A learner leaves muddy gumboots beside the bed and a dusty mask on the eating table. What hygiene problem does this cause?

Working:
1. Mud and dust hold germs.
2. The bed and the table are clean places that become dirty.
3. People can then pick up that dirt on clothes and food.

Answer: The dirty PPE contaminates the sleeping and eating places and can spread germs.

## Activity: Find dirt on used equipment
You will need: Used garden gloves or gumboots, Newspaper, Soap and water for the end of the lesson
1. Observe used equipment on newspaper and describe where dirt has collected.
2. Discuss how that dirt could reach food or a younger child if the item is left indoors.
3. Give three reasons cleaning will help.
4. Wash the item as a class if it is washable, then wash your hands.

## Practice
1. Give two reasons for cleaning PPE after work.
2. Where should muddy boots be cleaned?
3. Why is a school group responsible for cleaning shared gloves?

## Summary
• Dirty PPE carries germs into clean places.
• Cleaning protects people, makes the item work better and helps it last.
• Clean equipment outside the kitchen, then dry and store it.

### Answers to practice
1. Any two: to stop germs spreading, so it protects better next time, so it lasts longer, so damage can be seen, so the next user is safe.
2. Outside or in a washing area, not on the kitchen table or in the drinking-water basin.
3. The next group must find them clean and safe to wear.

PAGE 6: Lesson 5: Cleaning gumboots

LESSON 5: CLEANING GUMBOOTS
===========================

## What you will learn
• Clean gumboots safely.
• Dry and store gumboots so they stay fit to wear.

Curriculum outcomes: b) clean personal protective equipment for hygiene purposes

## Introduction
Gumboots meet the worst of the mud. A good clean knocks the dry dirt off, washes the rest with soap, and lets the boots dry where the rubber will not be spoiled.

## Notes
Clean gumboots after muddy work, before you wear them again, and before they are stored for another class. Do the work outside or at a tap where dirty water can drain away from drinking water.

Knock the soles together or scrape them with a stick to remove dry mud and stones. Check that no nail or thorn is stuck in the sole. Stones left in the tread cut the next floor you walk on and can pierce the boot.

Wash the outside with clean water and soap, using a brush kept for dirty footwear. Scrub the soles and the sides. Rinse. If the inside is muddy, wash the inside too and tip the water out. Do not use a chemical you cannot name. Soap and water are enough for farm mud.

Dry the boots upside down in a shady, airy place. Strong heat and a long time in fierce sun can crack rubber. Do not dry gumboots on a jiko or next to a flame. When they are dry inside and outside, stand them in their storage place, not on a bed and not in a closed wet sack.

While you wash, wear your own gloves if the boots came from an animal pen, and avoid splashing dirty water into your eyes. Wash your hands and the brush when you finish. If the class shares the boots, leave them clean and paired so the next person is not guessing which boot matches.

A boot with a hole or a split sole no longer keeps water out. Show it to the teacher or a parent. Wearing a split gumboot in a dirty pen gives false protection.

## Key words
• tread — the patterned part of a sole that touches the ground
• airy — a place where fresh air can move around the item

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Put these steps in order: rinse, scrape off dry mud, soap and scrub, dry in the shade upside down.

Working:
1. Dry mud is removed first so it does not turn into more mud in the water.
2. Soap and scrubbing come next, then rinsing.
3. Drying is last.

Answer: Scrape off dry mud, soap and scrub, rinse, then dry upside down in the shade.

## Activity: Wash a pair of gumboots
You will need: Gumboots, Stick or brush, Soap, Water, Gloves, A shady drying place
1. Scrape off dry mud and check the soles for stones or nails.
2. Scrub outside and, if needed, inside with soap and water.
3. Rinse and set the boots upside down in a shady airy place.
4. Wash your hands and the brush. Report any hole or split.

## Practice
1. Why scrape dry mud off gumboots before washing them?
2. Where should gumboots be dried, and why not beside a flame?
3. What should you do if you find a split in the sole?

## Summary
• Scrape, scrub with soap, rinse, and dry gumboots upside down in the shade.
• Do not dry rubber next to a fire.
• Report holes, and leave shared boots clean for the next user.

### Answers to practice
1. So that the dry dirt does not use up the clean water and turn into extra mud.
2. In a shady airy place. Strong heat can crack the rubber.
3. Show an adult. A split boot does not keep dirty water out.

PAGE 7: Lesson 6: Cleaning canvas shoes

LESSON 6: CLEANING CANVAS SHOES
===============================

## What you will learn
• Clean canvas shoes without spoiling their shape.
• Dry them so they do not stay damp.

Curriculum outcomes: b) clean personal protective equipment for hygiene purposes

## Introduction
Canvas shoes look tired when mud dries on the cloth. Washed and dried properly, the same pair is fit for the next day's work and does not smell.

## Notes
Clean canvas shoes when they are muddy, before the mud is ground deeper into the cloth. Take them outside. Remove the laces. Knock the soles together and brush off dry dirt with a stiff brush. Wiping wet mud straight into the cloth with a soaking rag pushes dirt further in.

Mix soap and a little clean water. Scrub the cloth upper with a brush or a cloth, including the heel and the edge of the sole. Wash the laces separately and rinse them. Rinse the shoes. Do not soak them for hours. Canvas that stays full of water takes a long time to dry and can lose its shape.

Stuff the toes with clean dry paper so the shoes keep their shape, if you have paper. Set them in the sun or in a warm breezy place, not on a cooker and not in a closed cupboard. Turn them so the inside dries as well as the outside. Hang the laces to dry. When everything is dry, thread the laces again and store the shoes off the floor.

Socks should be washed too. A clean shoe with a dirty wet sock puts the smell straight back. If the shoes are still damp in the morning, do not seal them in a plastic bag for the school day. Carry them in the open air or wear another pair.

Check the inside with your hand. Small stones cause blisters. A shoe with a flapping sole is no longer safe for garden work. Tell an adult.

Canvas shoes used for dirty work need this clean more often than shoes that only walk on a dry path. The method is the same. Soap, a brush, a rinse and a real drying time are the whole skill.

## Key words
• upper — the cloth part of a shoe above the sole
• laces — the strings that fasten a shoe

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Canvas shoes were washed and immediately sealed in a plastic bag. What is likely to happen, and what should have been done?

Working:
1. The shoes are still wet.
2. A closed bag stops them drying and they will smell.
3. They should be dried in the sun or a breeze first.

Answer: They will stay damp and smell. Dry them fully in the sun or a breezy place before storing them.

## Activity: Clean canvas shoes
You will need: Canvas shoes, Brush, Soap, Water, Newspaper or clean paper, A sunny or breezy drying spot
1. Remove the laces and brush off dry mud.
2. Scrub the uppers and the laces with soap and a little water, then rinse.
3. Stuff the toes with dry paper and dry the shoes in the sun or a breeze.
4. When they are dry, put the laces back and show the clean pair to your group.

## Practice
1. Why remove the laces before washing canvas shoes?
2. Why stuff the toes with dry paper?
3. Name two checks you make before wearing the shoes again.

## Summary
• Brush off dry mud, scrub with soap, and rinse.
• Dry canvas shoes in the sun or a breeze, not in a sealed bag.
• Wash the laces and the socks as well.

### Answers to practice
1. So that the laces and the cloth underneath them can be cleaned properly.
2. To help the shoes keep their shape while they dry.
3. They are fully dry, and there are no stones inside or damage to the sole.

PAGE 8: Lesson 7: Cleaning gloves, overalls, headgear and masks

LESSON 7: CLEANING GLOVES, OVERALLS, HEADGEAR AND MASKS
=======================================================

## What you will learn
• Clean washable gloves, overalls, headgear and cloth masks.
• Decide when a mask or glove should be thrown away instead.

Curriculum outcomes: b) clean personal protective equipment for hygiene purposes

## Introduction
Cloth items are cleaned in a different way from rubber boots. They need soap, a proper rinse and enough sun to dry them, or they stay damp and dirty against your skin.

## Notes
Wash reusable gloves in soap and water after dirty work. Turn them inside out if the inside is sweaty, wash both sides, rinse until the soap is gone, and hang them to dry. Do not dry gloves on the cooker. Put them away only when they are dry. If a glove has a hole, do not pretend it still protects you. Mend a small cloth tear if an adult can, or replace the glove. Thin disposable gloves are not washed and worn again. They are used once and put in the refuse, not in the compost.

An overall is washed like a dirty garment, but away from the family's drinking cups. Shake off dry dust outside. Soak and wash with soap, paying attention to cuffs and knees where dirt sticks. Rinse well so that soap does not irritate the skin next time. Dry the overall in the sun. Sunlight helps to freshen cloth. Iron it if your home irons work clothes, and hang it ready for the next job. A damp overall bundled under a bed will smell and can cause a rash.

Wash headgear that is made of cloth: caps and work headscarves. Brush a straw hat if it cannot be soaked, and leave it in the air. Do not share unwashed headgear.

A cloth dust mask is washed with soap, rinsed and dried fully before it is worn again. A mask that is still damp is unpleasant and less useful. Disposable dust masks are not washed. Replace them when they look dusty, get wet or tear. Never hand a used mask to another learner.

After you finish the washing, clean the basin if it is also used for food, or use a separate basin for work clothes. Wash your hands. The protective items are now ready to promote hygiene instead of spreading dirt.

## Key words
• reusable — able to be cleaned and used again
• disposable — meant to be used once and then thrown away

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Which of these should be washed, and which should be replaced: a muddy cloth apron, a torn disposable dust mask, sweaty reusable gloves?

Working:
1. The apron and the reusable gloves are made to be washed.
2. A torn disposable mask does not wash back into a safe mask.

Answer: Wash the apron and the gloves. Throw away the torn disposable mask and use a new one.

## Activity: Wash one cloth item of PPE
You will need: Reusable gloves, an apron, a cap or a cloth mask, Soap, Water, Drying line, Basin
1. Shake off dry dirt outside.
2. Wash the item with soap, including the parts that get dirtiest.
3. Rinse until the water runs clear and hang the item in the sun.
4. Label disposable items in a class display as 'do not wash' so nobody reuses them by mistake.

## Practice
1. How do you clean reusable gloves?
2. What should happen to a torn disposable dust mask?
3. Why dry an overall in the sun instead of bundling it while wet?
4. Why use care with the basin you used for work clothes?

## Summary
• Wash reusable cloth PPE with soap, rinse, and dry in the sun.
• Do not wash and reuse disposable masks or gloves.
• Store only items that are clean and dry.

### Answers to practice
1. Wash both sides with soap and water, rinse, and dry them completely.
2. It should be thrown away, not washed and shared.
3. Sun and air dry and freshen the cloth. A wet bundle smells and can irritate the skin.
4. If it is also a food basin, it must be cleaned so that dirt from the clothes does not reach food.

PAGE 9: Lesson 8: A display of clean protective equipment

LESSON 8: A DISPLAY OF CLEAN PROTECTIVE EQUIPMENT
=================================================

## What you will learn
• Prepare a display of cleaned PPE.
• Explain how clean equipment promotes hygiene.

Curriculum outcomes: c) appreciate clean personal protective equipment in promoting hygiene

## Introduction
A display turns the cleaning you have done into something the class can see. Clean gumboots, dry canvas shoes and a washed overall make the point better than a talk about dirt.

## Notes
Appreciating clean PPE means you value it enough to keep it clean and to show others why that matters. A class display is a simple way to do this. Choose items that have actually been cleaned: a pair of gumboots, canvas shoes, gloves, a cloth mask or a labelled picture of a disposable mask, headgear and an overall or apron.

Set the display on a clean table or along a wall, with newspaper or a cloth underneath. Each item needs a label with its name, the work it is used for, and one cleaning rule. For example: 'Gumboots. Used in mud. Scrape, wash, dry in the shade.' Arrange items so that people can walk past without stepping on them. Do not display wet, muddy equipment as if it were the goal.

Prepare a short presentation in your group. Say what the item protects, how you cleaned it, and how that cleaning promotes hygiene. Mention safety during cleaning: no splashing into eyes, no unknown chemicals, hands washed afterwards. Invite another group to ask one question.

The display is also a check. If the canvas shoes are still damp, they are not ready. If the gloves have holes, they should be in a 'needs repair' space, not in the 'ready to wear' space. Honesty makes the display useful.

After the presentation, store the items properly. Boots stand in the shade store. Cloth items hang dry. Masks that must be thrown away go into the refuse, not back onto the display as if they were clean. The end of the lesson is a tidy room and equipment that the next class can trust.

At home, you may not make a display, but you can keep one clean spot by the door where boots are washed and overalls hang. That spot is a small daily reminder of the same idea.

## Key words
• display — a neat arrangement that shows work so other people can learn from it
• label — a short written note that names an item and gives a rule

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Write a three-part label for canvas shoes that have been cleaned.

Working:
1. Name the item.
2. Say what work it is for.
3. Give the cleaning rule.

Answer: Canvas shoes. For dry work. Brush, wash with soap, dry in the sun.

## Activity: Display the cleaned equipment
You will need: Cleaned PPE, Cards, Pens, A table or wall space, Cloth or newspaper
1. Agree which items are truly clean and dry enough to display.
2. Write a label for each: name, use and one cleaning rule.
3. Present the display to another group and answer a question about hygiene.
4. Store the items correctly when the display is finished.

## Practice
1. What three things should a PPE label say?
2. Why should wet boots not be placed in the 'ready' part of the display?
3. How does a display help the class appreciate clean PPE?

## Summary
• Display only equipment that has been cleaned and dried.
• Label each item with its name, use and a cleaning rule.
• Store everything properly after the presentation.

### Answers to practice
1. The name of the item, the work it is used for, and one cleaning rule.
2. They are not finished. Wet equipment is not yet clean enough to store or reuse.
3. It shows real cleaned items and the rules, so learners value keeping equipment fit to wear.
pages.quiz:
REVISION QUIZ — 3.3 CLEANING PERSONAL PROTECTIVE EQUIPMENT
========================================

Answer all the questions, then mark yourself on the Answers tab.

1. Which list names personal protective equipment?
   A. Plate, cup and spoon
   B. Gloves, dust mask, gumboots, headgear, overall and canvas shoes
   C. Broom, mop and dustpan
   D. Needle, thread and scissors

2. What does a dust mask protect?
   A. The knees
   B. The nose and mouth from dust
   C. The eyes from bright books
   D. The feet from mud

3. Which footwear is suitable in a muddy animal pen?
   A. Canvas shoes
   B. Gumboots
   C. Open sandals
   D. Socks only

4. Why should dirty gumboots not be left beside the bed?

5. What is the correct order for cleaning muddy gumboots?
   A. Dry them on the fire, then wear them
   B. Scrape off mud, wash with soap, rinse, dry in the shade
   C. Soak them in drinking water indoors
   D. Paint them and store them wet

6. Why are canvas shoes dried before they are stored in a bag?

7. What should be done with a torn disposable dust mask?
   A. Wash it and share it
   B. Throw it away and use another
   C. Hang it in the kitchen
   D. Use it as a handkerchief

8. Why wash reusable gloves on both sides?

9. How does cleaning PPE promote hygiene?

10. A good PPE label includes which three points?
   A. Price, shop and colour only
   B. Name, the work it is used for, and a cleaning rule
   C. The owner's age, class and game
   D. Nothing, because labels spread germs
pages.answers:
ANSWERS — 3.3 CLEANING PERSONAL PROTECTIVE EQUIPMENT
========================================

1. B. Gloves, dust mask, gumboots, headgear, overall and canvas shoes
   These six items are the everyday PPE in this sub-strand.

2. B. The nose and mouth from dust
   A dust mask covers the nose and mouth so that less dust is breathed in.

3. B. Gumboots
   Gumboots are waterproof and protect the feet in mud and dirt.

4. They carry mud and germs into a clean place.
   PPE should be cleaned and stored so that it does not contaminate the house.

5. B. Scrape off mud, wash with soap, rinse, dry in the shade
   Dry mud comes off first. Soap, rinsing and shady drying protect both hygiene and the rubber.

6. Damp shoes kept closed will not dry and will start to smell.
   Sun or a breeze dries the cloth so the shoes stay fresh.

7. B. Throw it away and use another
   Disposable masks are not washed and reused. A tear means it no longer protects.

8. The outside meets dirt and the inside meets sweat, so both need cleaning.
   Then rinse and dry them fully before storage.

9. It removes dirt and germs so the equipment does not spread them to people, food or the next wearer.
   Clean, dry equipment protects better and keeps the home cleaner.

10. B. Name, the work it is used for, and a cleaning rule
   The label teaches the name, the use and how to keep the item clean.

studyPages.title: Overview
studyPages.body:
OVERVIEW
========

Personal protective equipment only protects you when it is clean and in good condition. In this sub-strand you will identify gloves, dust masks, gumboots, headgear, overalls and canvas shoes, learn how to clean them, and display clean equipment as a reminder that hygiene includes the things you wear for work.

## Strand 3.0: Hygiene Practices
Sub-strand 3.3: Cleaning Personal Protective Equipment
Suggested lessons: 9

## Learning outcomes
By the end of the sub-strand, the learner should be able to:
a) identify personal protective equipment in day to day life
b) clean personal protective equipment for hygiene purposes
c) appreciate clean personal protective equipment in promoting hygiene

## Key inquiry questions
1. How does cleaning of personal protective equipment promote hygiene?

## Core competencies
• Digital literacy: use of digital technology as learners search for information on personal protective equipment.

## Values
• Responsibility: safety and care of self as learners clean personal protective equipment.

## Pertinent and contemporary issues
• Personal safety as learners exercise caution while undertaking cleaning activity.

## Links to other learning areas
• Learners relate use of personal protective equipment to personal safety skills learnt in Science and Technology.

## Source
• KICD Grade 4 Agriculture Curriculum Design (Revised 2024) — Strand 3.0 Hygiene Practices, Sub-strand 3.3 Cleaning Personal Protective Equipment

studyPages.title: Lesson 1: What personal protective equipment is
studyPages.body:
LESSON 1: WHAT PERSONAL PROTECTIVE EQUIPMENT IS
===============================================

## What you will learn
• Explain what personal protective equipment is.
• Name the common items used in day-to-day work.

Curriculum outcomes: a) identify personal protective equipment in day to day life

## Introduction
Before you handle compost, sweep a dusty store or walk through a muddy pen, you put something on so that the dirt meets the equipment first. That clothing and gear is personal protective equipment.

## Notes
Personal protective equipment, shortened to PPE, is what you wear to protect your body while you work. It is personal because it guards the wearer. It is protective because it stops injuries and blocks mud, dust, thorns and waste. In day-to-day life at home, at school and on the farm, the items you should be able to name are gloves, dust masks, gumboots, headgear, overalls and canvas shoes.

Each item covers a different part of the body. Gloves cover the hands. A dust mask covers the nose and mouth. Gumboots and canvas shoes cover the feet. Headgear covers the hair and shades the head. An overall covers the clothes and much of the body. You do not need every item for every job. You need the item that matches the risk.

PPE is also a hygiene matter. Dirt that stays on your shirt or under your nails travels into the house and onto food. Equipment that catches that dirt can be removed and cleaned at the door. In that way, protective equipment supports the personal hygiene and domestic hygiene you have already studied.

The equipment must be the right size. Gloves that fall off do not protect. Gumboots that are far too big can make you trip. A mask that does not cover the nose is only a decoration. Equipment must also be whole. A hole in a glove lets dirt straight onto the skin.

You may see other protective items on adults, such as goggles or helmets, in workshops and on building sites. In this sub-strand, concentrate on the six everyday items so that you can identify them in real work and know which ones you will learn to clean.

Look around the school store, the garden and your home. Point to each item by its proper name before you use it.

## Key words
• personal protective equipment — gear worn to protect the body during work
• PPE — the short name for personal protective equipment

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Name the PPE that protects the hands, the feet in mud, and the nose during dusty work.

Working:
1. Hands are covered by gloves.
2. Feet in mud are protected by gumboots.
3. The nose and mouth are protected by a dust mask.

Answer: Gloves, gumboots and a dust mask.

## Activity: Identify protective equipment
You will need: Real items or pictures of gloves, dust masks, gumboots, headgear, an overall and canvas shoes, Exercise book
1. Observe each item and name it.
2. Say which part of the body it protects.
3. Search a school poster, a book or a digital device, if one is available, for one more fact about that item.
4. Write the six names and one job for each.

## Practice
1. What is personal protective equipment?
2. List six common PPE items in day-to-day work.
3. Why does PPE need to fit and to be free of holes?

## Summary
• PPE protects the body during work.
• The everyday items are gloves, dust masks, gumboots, headgear, overalls and canvas shoes.
• Each item must fit and be in good condition.

### Answers to practice
1. Gear worn to protect the body while working.
2. Gloves, dust masks, gumboots, headgear, overalls and canvas shoes.
3. If it falls off or has holes, dirt and injury can still reach the body.

studyPages.title: Lesson 2: Gloves, dust masks and headgear
studyPages.body:
LESSON 2: GLOVES, DUST MASKS AND HEADGEAR
=========================================

## What you will learn
• Describe gloves, dust masks and headgear.
• Match each item to suitable work.

Curriculum outcomes: a) identify personal protective equipment in day to day life

## Introduction
Hands, lungs and hair meet dirt in different ways. A glove does not stop dust you breathe, and a hat does not keep compost off your fingers. You choose the item for the part of the body at risk.

## Notes
Gloves protect the hands from dirt, thorns, rough stalks and waste. Garden gloves are often made of cloth or rubber. Rubber gloves are better when the work is wet. Cloth gloves are better for dry weeding, but they soak up water and then hold dirt against the skin. Gloves do not replace hand washing. When you pull them off, your hands can still pick up what was on the outside, so you wash with soap afterwards.

A dust mask covers the nose and mouth. It reduces the dust you breathe when you sweep a dry store, shake dry fodder or work where fine dust rises. It is not a swimming mask and it is not medicine. A cloth mask can be washed. Some thin dust masks are meant to be thrown away when they are dusty, wet or torn. A mask that has gaps at the sides lets dust pass. Do not share masks. Do not wear a mask that is so dirty you are breathing through mud.

Headgear means a cap, hat or clean headscarf worn for work. It keeps dust, seeds and dry leaves out of the hair and shades the head from strong sun. Hair that is covered is also less likely to drop into food if you move from the garden to helping in the kitchen, though you still wash your hands. Headgear for work should be washable. A school hat and a work hat can be the same kind of item, but a hat used in a dirty pen should be cleaned before it is worn to a meal.

These three items are often forgotten because the work looks small. Pulling weeds still drives soil under the nails. Sweeping a store still fills the air with dust. Name the item, wear it for the right job, and take it off before you sit down to eat.

## Key words
• gloves — coverings worn on the hands during dirty or rough work
• headgear — a cap, hat or headscarf worn to protect the head and hair

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Which items fit these jobs: sorting dry maize in a dusty store, washing a muddy tool, weeding under a hot sun?

Working:
1. Dusty sorting needs a dust mask.
2. A muddy wash needs gloves, preferably ones that can get wet.
3. Hot sun and hair full of bits of plant call for headgear.

Answer: Dust mask for the store, gloves for the muddy tool, headgear for weeding in the sun.

## Activity: Match three items to real jobs
You will need: Gloves, Dust mask, Cap or headscarf, Job cards
1. Lay the three items on the table and observe how each is worn.
2. Match them to jobs the class suggests from home and school.
3. Practise putting gloves on and taking them off without touching the dirty side with your bare palm as much as you can.
4. Wash your hands after the demonstration.

## Practice
1. Why do you wash your hands after taking off gloves?
2. When should a disposable dust mask be thrown away?
3. What does headgear protect you from during garden work?

## Summary
• Gloves protect hands, masks reduce dust breathed in, and headgear covers the hair.
• Choose the item that matches the job.
• Do not share masks, and wash hands after removing gloves.

### Answers to practice
1. Dirt from the outside of the gloves can get onto your skin as you remove them.
2. When it is dusty, wet or torn.
3. Sun, dust and bits of plants in the hair.

studyPages.title: Lesson 3: Gumboots, overalls and canvas shoes
studyPages.body:
LESSON 3: GUMBOOTS, OVERALLS AND CANVAS SHOES
=============================================

## What you will learn
• Describe gumboots, overalls and canvas shoes.
• Choose footwear and body covering for wet and dry work.

Curriculum outcomes: a) identify personal protective equipment in day to day life

## Introduction
Canvas shoes are light and useful on a dry path. They are a poor choice in a flooded pen. Gumboots are the opposite. Knowing the difference keeps your feet and your clothes clean.

## Notes
Gumboots are waterproof boots, usually rubber, that cover the foot and the lower leg. Wear them in mud, wet grass, animal houses, and places where sharp rubbish or hidden stones may cut an open shoe. Tuck long trousers into them or wear them under an overall so that mud does not run down inside. Gumboots that are full of yesterday's mud are not protecting hygiene. They are carrying the pen into the house.

An overall is a garment worn over ordinary clothes. It takes splashes, dust and dung so that your uniform or home clothes stay clean. Button or zip it properly. Sleeves that flap can catch on tools. After dirty work, take the overall off before you sit on a bed or a classroom chair. If you only own an apron, use the apron in the same spirit: it is body covering for the front of your clothes during cleaning or cooking.

Canvas shoes are cloth shoes with a rubber sole. They suit dry sweeping, classroom duties and dry garden work. They are cooler and lighter than gumboots. They are not waterproof. Wet canvas holds water, dries slowly and can smell if it is left in a bag. Wear socks so that the shoe does not rub the skin. Canvas shoes used as PPE should be kept for work if you can, so that the pair you wear to a clean room stays cleaner.

Choose footwear by looking at the ground. Dry and fairly clean ground: canvas shoes. Mud, dung or water: gumboots. Add the overall when the whole body, not only the feet, will meet dirt. School uniform alone is not protective equipment for a cowshed.

All three items last longer when they are cleaned and dried after use. The next lessons show how. For identification, you should be able to point to each one and say what work it is for.

## Key words
• gumboots — waterproof rubber boots that protect the feet and lower legs
• canvas shoes — light cloth shoes with rubber soles for dry work
• overall — a garment worn over clothes to keep them clean

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A learner wears canvas shoes and a school uniform to wash out a muddy goat pen. What is wrong with the choice?

Working:
1. The ground is wet and dirty.
2. Canvas shoes soak up muddy water.
3. The uniform has no covering, so it will carry dirt back to the house.

Answer: Gumboots and an overall would protect the feet and clothes. Canvas shoes and uniform are for cleaner, drier work.

## Activity: Choose footwear and covering for two jobs
You will need: Pictures or real gumboots, canvas shoes and an overall, Two job cards: dry sweeping and washing a pen
1. Observe how gumboots, canvas shoes and an overall are made.
2. Decide which to wear for dry sweeping and which for a wet pen.
3. Explain your choice to another pair of learners.
4. List one problem caused by wearing the wrong shoes.

## Practice
1. When are gumboots a better choice than canvas shoes?
2. What is the job of an overall?
3. Why are wet canvas shoes a hygiene problem if they are left in a closed bag?

## Summary
• Gumboots are for wet and muddy work. Canvas shoes are for dry work.
• An overall keeps dirt off your clothes.
• Choose the covering that matches the ground and the job.

### Answers to practice
1. In mud, water, animal houses and places with sharp rubbish.
2. To cover ordinary clothes so that dirt from work does not spoil them.
3. They stay damp and start to smell, and they do not dry.

studyPages.title: Lesson 4: Why protective equipment must be cleaned
studyPages.body:
LESSON 4: WHY PROTECTIVE EQUIPMENT MUST BE CLEANED
==================================================

## What you will learn
• Explain how dirty PPE spreads dirt and germs.
• Give reasons for cleaning equipment after work.

Curriculum outcomes: a) identify personal protective equipment in day to day life; c) appreciate clean personal protective equipment in promoting hygiene

## Introduction
Gumboots caked with dung do not stop being dirty when you step into the kitchen. If the dirt is not washed off, the equipment carries the pen, the store or the latrine into the next place.

## Notes
Cleaning PPE promotes hygiene because it removes the dirt the equipment was worn to catch. That dirt may include soil, animal droppings, food waste, grease and dust. Germs travel with it. A dirty glove on a clean table, or a dusty mask on a bed, undoes the washing you did on your hands and the sweeping you did on the floor.

There are four clear reasons to clean the equipment. First, clean PPE does not spread germs to people, food and furniture. Second, it protects you better next time. A blocked mask is hard to breathe through, and a greasy glove slips. Third, clean equipment lasts longer. Mud left on rubber cracks and rots cloth. Fourth, you can see damage once the dirt is off. A nail in a boot, a hole in a glove or a torn strap shows up on a clean item.

Cleaning also shows respect for the next user. At school, gumboots and gloves may be shared across groups. The group that finishes must leave them fit for the group that follows. That is part of caring for other learners' safety.

Dirty equipment should be cleaned outside or in a washing area, not on the kitchen table and not in the drinking-water basin. Scrape dry mud off first so that you do not waste water. Use soap where the item allows it. Dry the item before you store it. Folding a wet overall into a plastic bag keeps it sour.

Appreciate clean PPE by treating it as part of the job, not as an extra you skip when you are tired. The last minutes of work are washing the boots, hanging the overall and washing your own hands. Then the house stays as clean as you left it.

## Key words
• contaminate — to spread dirt or germs onto something clean
• store — to keep equipment in a set place when it is not being worn

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A learner leaves muddy gumboots beside the bed and a dusty mask on the eating table. What hygiene problem does this cause?

Working:
1. Mud and dust hold germs.
2. The bed and the table are clean places that become dirty.
3. People can then pick up that dirt on clothes and food.

Answer: The dirty PPE contaminates the sleeping and eating places and can spread germs.

## Activity: Find dirt on used equipment
You will need: Used garden gloves or gumboots, Newspaper, Soap and water for the end of the lesson
1. Observe used equipment on newspaper and describe where dirt has collected.
2. Discuss how that dirt could reach food or a younger child if the item is left indoors.
3. Give three reasons cleaning will help.
4. Wash the item as a class if it is washable, then wash your hands.

## Practice
1. Give two reasons for cleaning PPE after work.
2. Where should muddy boots be cleaned?
3. Why is a school group responsible for cleaning shared gloves?

## Summary
• Dirty PPE carries germs into clean places.
• Cleaning protects people, makes the item work better and helps it last.
• Clean equipment outside the kitchen, then dry and store it.

### Answers to practice
1. Any two: to stop germs spreading, so it protects better next time, so it lasts longer, so damage can be seen, so the next user is safe.
2. Outside or in a washing area, not on the kitchen table or in the drinking-water basin.
3. The next group must find them clean and safe to wear.

studyPages.title: Lesson 5: Cleaning gumboots
studyPages.body:
LESSON 5: CLEANING GUMBOOTS
===========================

## What you will learn
• Clean gumboots safely.
• Dry and store gumboots so they stay fit to wear.

Curriculum outcomes: b) clean personal protective equipment for hygiene purposes

## Introduction
Gumboots meet the worst of the mud. A good clean knocks the dry dirt off, washes the rest with soap, and lets the boots dry where the rubber will not be spoiled.

## Notes
Clean gumboots after muddy work, before you wear them again, and before they are stored for another class. Do the work outside or at a tap where dirty water can drain away from drinking water.

Knock the soles together or scrape them with a stick to remove dry mud and stones. Check that no nail or thorn is stuck in the sole. Stones left in the tread cut the next floor you walk on and can pierce the boot.

Wash the outside with clean water and soap, using a brush kept for dirty footwear. Scrub the soles and the sides. Rinse. If the inside is muddy, wash the inside too and tip the water out. Do not use a chemical you cannot name. Soap and water are enough for farm mud.

Dry the boots upside down in a shady, airy place. Strong heat and a long time in fierce sun can crack rubber. Do not dry gumboots on a jiko or next to a flame. When they are dry inside and outside, stand them in their storage place, not on a bed and not in a closed wet sack.

While you wash, wear your own gloves if the boots came from an animal pen, and avoid splashing dirty water into your eyes. Wash your hands and the brush when you finish. If the class shares the boots, leave them clean and paired so the next person is not guessing which boot matches.

A boot with a hole or a split sole no longer keeps water out. Show it to the teacher or a parent. Wearing a split gumboot in a dirty pen gives false protection.

## Key words
• tread — the patterned part of a sole that touches the ground
• airy — a place where fresh air can move around the item

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Put these steps in order: rinse, scrape off dry mud, soap and scrub, dry in the shade upside down.

Working:
1. Dry mud is removed first so it does not turn into more mud in the water.
2. Soap and scrubbing come next, then rinsing.
3. Drying is last.

Answer: Scrape off dry mud, soap and scrub, rinse, then dry upside down in the shade.

## Activity: Wash a pair of gumboots
You will need: Gumboots, Stick or brush, Soap, Water, Gloves, A shady drying place
1. Scrape off dry mud and check the soles for stones or nails.
2. Scrub outside and, if needed, inside with soap and water.
3. Rinse and set the boots upside down in a shady airy place.
4. Wash your hands and the brush. Report any hole or split.

## Practice
1. Why scrape dry mud off gumboots before washing them?
2. Where should gumboots be dried, and why not beside a flame?
3. What should you do if you find a split in the sole?

## Summary
• Scrape, scrub with soap, rinse, and dry gumboots upside down in the shade.
• Do not dry rubber next to a fire.
• Report holes, and leave shared boots clean for the next user.

### Answers to practice
1. So that the dry dirt does not use up the clean water and turn into extra mud.
2. In a shady airy place. Strong heat can crack the rubber.
3. Show an adult. A split boot does not keep dirty water out.

studyPages.title: Lesson 6: Cleaning canvas shoes
studyPages.body:
LESSON 6: CLEANING CANVAS SHOES
===============================

## What you will learn
• Clean canvas shoes without spoiling their shape.
• Dry them so they do not stay damp.

Curriculum outcomes: b) clean personal protective equipment for hygiene purposes

## Introduction
Canvas shoes look tired when mud dries on the cloth. Washed and dried properly, the same pair is fit for the next day's work and does not smell.

## Notes
Clean canvas shoes when they are muddy, before the mud is ground deeper into the cloth. Take them outside. Remove the laces. Knock the soles together and brush off dry dirt with a stiff brush. Wiping wet mud straight into the cloth with a soaking rag pushes dirt further in.

Mix soap and a little clean water. Scrub the cloth upper with a brush or a cloth, including the heel and the edge of the sole. Wash the laces separately and rinse them. Rinse the shoes. Do not soak them for hours. Canvas that stays full of water takes a long time to dry and can lose its shape.

Stuff the toes with clean dry paper so the shoes keep their shape, if you have paper. Set them in the sun or in a warm breezy place, not on a cooker and not in a closed cupboard. Turn them so the inside dries as well as the outside. Hang the laces to dry. When everything is dry, thread the laces again and store the shoes off the floor.

Socks should be washed too. A clean shoe with a dirty wet sock puts the smell straight back. If the shoes are still damp in the morning, do not seal them in a plastic bag for the school day. Carry them in the open air or wear another pair.

Check the inside with your hand. Small stones cause blisters. A shoe with a flapping sole is no longer safe for garden work. Tell an adult.

Canvas shoes used for dirty work need this clean more often than shoes that only walk on a dry path. The method is the same. Soap, a brush, a rinse and a real drying time are the whole skill.

## Key words
• upper — the cloth part of a shoe above the sole
• laces — the strings that fasten a shoe

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Canvas shoes were washed and immediately sealed in a plastic bag. What is likely to happen, and what should have been done?

Working:
1. The shoes are still wet.
2. A closed bag stops them drying and they will smell.
3. They should be dried in the sun or a breeze first.

Answer: They will stay damp and smell. Dry them fully in the sun or a breezy place before storing them.

## Activity: Clean canvas shoes
You will need: Canvas shoes, Brush, Soap, Water, Newspaper or clean paper, A sunny or breezy drying spot
1. Remove the laces and brush off dry mud.
2. Scrub the uppers and the laces with soap and a little water, then rinse.
3. Stuff the toes with dry paper and dry the shoes in the sun or a breeze.
4. When they are dry, put the laces back and show the clean pair to your group.

## Practice
1. Why remove the laces before washing canvas shoes?
2. Why stuff the toes with dry paper?
3. Name two checks you make before wearing the shoes again.

## Summary
• Brush off dry mud, scrub with soap, and rinse.
• Dry canvas shoes in the sun or a breeze, not in a sealed bag.
• Wash the laces and the socks as well.

### Answers to practice
1. So that the laces and the cloth underneath them can be cleaned properly.
2. To help the shoes keep their shape while they dry.
3. They are fully dry, and there are no stones inside or damage to the sole.

studyPages.title: Lesson 7: Cleaning gloves, overalls, headgear and masks
studyPages.body:
LESSON 7: CLEANING GLOVES, OVERALLS, HEADGEAR AND MASKS
=======================================================

## What you will learn
• Clean washable gloves, overalls, headgear and cloth masks.
• Decide when a mask or glove should be thrown away instead.

Curriculum outcomes: b) clean personal protective equipment for hygiene purposes

## Introduction
Cloth items are cleaned in a different way from rubber boots. They need soap, a proper rinse and enough sun to dry them, or they stay damp and dirty against your skin.

## Notes
Wash reusable gloves in soap and water after dirty work. Turn them inside out if the inside is sweaty, wash both sides, rinse until the soap is gone, and hang them to dry. Do not dry gloves on the cooker. Put them away only when they are dry. If a glove has a hole, do not pretend it still protects you. Mend a small cloth tear if an adult can, or replace the glove. Thin disposable gloves are not washed and worn again. They are used once and put in the refuse, not in the compost.

An overall is washed like a dirty garment, but away from the family's drinking cups. Shake off dry dust outside. Soak and wash with soap, paying attention to cuffs and knees where dirt sticks. Rinse well so that soap does not irritate the skin next time. Dry the overall in the sun. Sunlight helps to freshen cloth. Iron it if your home irons work clothes, and hang it ready for the next job. A damp overall bundled under a bed will smell and can cause a rash.

Wash headgear that is made of cloth: caps and work headscarves. Brush a straw hat if it cannot be soaked, and leave it in the air. Do not share unwashed headgear.

A cloth dust mask is washed with soap, rinsed and dried fully before it is worn again. A mask that is still damp is unpleasant and less useful. Disposable dust masks are not washed. Replace them when they look dusty, get wet or tear. Never hand a used mask to another learner.

After you finish the washing, clean the basin if it is also used for food, or use a separate basin for work clothes. Wash your hands. The protective items are now ready to promote hygiene instead of spreading dirt.

## Key words
• reusable — able to be cleaned and used again
• disposable — meant to be used once and then thrown away

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Which of these should be washed, and which should be replaced: a muddy cloth apron, a torn disposable dust mask, sweaty reusable gloves?

Working:
1. The apron and the reusable gloves are made to be washed.
2. A torn disposable mask does not wash back into a safe mask.

Answer: Wash the apron and the gloves. Throw away the torn disposable mask and use a new one.

## Activity: Wash one cloth item of PPE
You will need: Reusable gloves, an apron, a cap or a cloth mask, Soap, Water, Drying line, Basin
1. Shake off dry dirt outside.
2. Wash the item with soap, including the parts that get dirtiest.
3. Rinse until the water runs clear and hang the item in the sun.
4. Label disposable items in a class display as 'do not wash' so nobody reuses them by mistake.

## Practice
1. How do you clean reusable gloves?
2. What should happen to a torn disposable dust mask?
3. Why dry an overall in the sun instead of bundling it while wet?
4. Why use care with the basin you used for work clothes?

## Summary
• Wash reusable cloth PPE with soap, rinse, and dry in the sun.
• Do not wash and reuse disposable masks or gloves.
• Store only items that are clean and dry.

### Answers to practice
1. Wash both sides with soap and water, rinse, and dry them completely.
2. It should be thrown away, not washed and shared.
3. Sun and air dry and freshen the cloth. A wet bundle smells and can irritate the skin.
4. If it is also a food basin, it must be cleaned so that dirt from the clothes does not reach food.

studyPages.title: Lesson 8: A display of clean protective equipment
studyPages.body:
LESSON 8: A DISPLAY OF CLEAN PROTECTIVE EQUIPMENT
=================================================

## What you will learn
• Prepare a display of cleaned PPE.
• Explain how clean equipment promotes hygiene.

Curriculum outcomes: c) appreciate clean personal protective equipment in promoting hygiene

## Introduction
A display turns the cleaning you have done into something the class can see. Clean gumboots, dry canvas shoes and a washed overall make the point better than a talk about dirt.

## Notes
Appreciating clean PPE means you value it enough to keep it clean and to show others why that matters. A class display is a simple way to do this. Choose items that have actually been cleaned: a pair of gumboots, canvas shoes, gloves, a cloth mask or a labelled picture of a disposable mask, headgear and an overall or apron.

Set the display on a clean table or along a wall, with newspaper or a cloth underneath. Each item needs a label with its name, the work it is used for, and one cleaning rule. For example: 'Gumboots. Used in mud. Scrape, wash, dry in the shade.' Arrange items so that people can walk past without stepping on them. Do not display wet, muddy equipment as if it were the goal.

Prepare a short presentation in your group. Say what the item protects, how you cleaned it, and how that cleaning promotes hygiene. Mention safety during cleaning: no splashing into eyes, no unknown chemicals, hands washed afterwards. Invite another group to ask one question.

The display is also a check. If the canvas shoes are still damp, they are not ready. If the gloves have holes, they should be in a 'needs repair' space, not in the 'ready to wear' space. Honesty makes the display useful.

After the presentation, store the items properly. Boots stand in the shade store. Cloth items hang dry. Masks that must be thrown away go into the refuse, not back onto the display as if they were clean. The end of the lesson is a tidy room and equipment that the next class can trust.

At home, you may not make a display, but you can keep one clean spot by the door where boots are washed and overalls hang. That spot is a small daily reminder of the same idea.

## Key words
• display — a neat arrangement that shows work so other people can learn from it
• label — a short written note that names an item and gives a rule

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Write a three-part label for canvas shoes that have been cleaned.

Working:
1. Name the item.
2. Say what work it is for.
3. Give the cleaning rule.

Answer: Canvas shoes. For dry work. Brush, wash with soap, dry in the sun.

## Activity: Display the cleaned equipment
You will need: Cleaned PPE, Cards, Pens, A table or wall space, Cloth or newspaper
1. Agree which items are truly clean and dry enough to display.
2. Write a label for each: name, use and one cleaning rule.
3. Present the display to another group and answer a question about hygiene.
4. Store the items correctly when the display is finished.

## Practice
1. What three things should a PPE label say?
2. Why should wet boots not be placed in the 'ready' part of the display?
3. How does a display help the class appreciate clean PPE?

## Summary
• Display only equipment that has been cleaned and dried.
• Label each item with its name, use and a cleaning rule.
• Store everything properly after the presentation.

### Answers to practice
1. The name of the item, the work it is used for, and one cleaning rule.
2. They are not finished. Wet equipment is not yet clean enough to store or reuse.
3. It shows real cleaned items and the rules, so learners value keeping equipment fit to wear.

questions.question: Which list names personal protective equipment?
options: Gloves, dust mask, gumboots, headgear, overall and canvas shoes
questions.explanation: These six items are the everyday PPE in this sub-strand.

questions.question: What does a dust mask protect?
options: The nose and mouth from dust
questions.explanation: A dust mask covers the nose and mouth so that less dust is breathed in.

questions.question: Which footwear is suitable in a muddy animal pen?
questions.explanation: Gumboots are waterproof and protect the feet in mud and dirt.

questions.question: Why should dirty gumboots not be left beside the bed?
questions.answer: They carry mud and germs into a clean place.
questions.explanation: PPE should be cleaned and stored so that it does not contaminate the house.

questions.question: What is the correct order for cleaning muddy gumboots?
options: Dry them on the fire, then wear them
Scrape off mud, wash with soap, rinse, dry in the shade
Soak them in drinking water indoors
Paint them and store them wet
questions.explanation: Dry mud comes off first. Soap, rinsing and shady drying protect both hygiene and the rubber.

questions.question: Why are canvas shoes dried before they are stored in a bag?
questions.answer: Damp shoes kept closed will not dry and will start to smell.
questions.explanation: Sun or a breeze dries the cloth so the shoes stay fresh.

questions.question: What should be done with a torn disposable dust mask?
options: Throw it away and use another
questions.explanation: Disposable masks are not washed and reused. A tear means it no longer protects.

questions.question: Why wash reusable gloves on both sides?
questions.answer: The outside meets dirt and the inside meets sweat, so both need cleaning.
questions.explanation: Then rinse and dry them fully before storage.

questions.question: How does cleaning PPE promote hygiene?
questions.answer: It removes dirt and germs so the equipment does not spread them to people, food or the next wearer.
questions.explanation: Clean, dry equipment protects better and keeps the home cleaner.

questions.question: A good PPE label includes which three points?
options: Name, the work it is used for, and a cleaning rule
The owner's age, class and game
questions.explanation: The label teaches the name, the use and how to keep the item clean.
